title: Classification of Sir2-HerA systems reveals a multilayered regulatory cascade gating the type III antiphage activity.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Read the open-access full text (91 kB) including the data availability statement and methods; the statement says only 'available in the article and in its online supplementary material' with no repository accession. Europe PMC's supplementaryFiles endpoint timed out twice (cached failure), and the NCBI PMC open-access package service returns 404 for PMC13434337, so no machine-readable file listing exists. Text-mined identifiers are only an existing PDB structure (8J4U, from earlier work) and a preprint DOI - no GEO/SRA/BioProject/Zenodo/Dryad deposit.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: All counts: 2,892 Sir2-domain proteins pulled from NCBI, clustered by CD-HIT at 70% identity into 58 clusters; 8 of those clusters have a neighbouring HerA gene; 2,289 public E. coli genomes mined; 816 lab E. coli isolates used as PCR templates; one representative system per cluster challenged with 110 E. coli phages. The three supplementary tables are described in the text as primer sequences (S1), DNA substrate sequences for the enzyme assays (S2), and a phage/gene list (S3); the quantitative antiphage protection data is presented as a heat map in Figure 1C.

a1_downloadable.note: No login or access application, so not an access failure; but there is no deposited dataset - everything is inside the article PDF and three supplementary files, and I could not retrieve the supplement (Europe PMC supplementaryFiles timed out twice; PMC open-access package 404).

a2_label_is_a_column.note: FAILS. The thing a model would predict - how strongly each Sir2-HerA system restricts each phage - exists only as colour in the Figure 1C heat map. The named supplementary tables are primers, DNA substrate sequences and a phage list, so the label would have to be reconstructed by reading pixel values off a figure image. That is construction by inference, not a column.

a3_inputs_present.note: Inputs are obtainable in principle: Sir2 and HerA protein sequences come from NCBI and phage genomes are public, but the paper gives no sequence file, so even the inputs need identifier resolution from a figure/table that I could not open.

a4_units_stated.note: The protection readout is 'restriction efficiency' from tenfold serial-dilution plaque assays (efficiency of plating, a fold-change), described in methods but never tabulated with a units column; the heat map scale is only in the figure legend.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAILS. At most 8 representative systems x 110 phages = 880 heat-map cells, and the unit that matters for prediction is the defense system, of which there are 8 (4 with activity). Far under the ~400-row floor for classification.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: <10 MB (a few supplementary tables plus ~2,892 protein sequences)
a6_fits_laptop.note: Trivially small; size is not the problem here.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Cannot be checked at all - no data file was retrievable, so paper, API and download cannot be compared. Per the checklist this is an unverifiable-count situation, not a confirmed match.

a8_label_provenance.note: The one large label in the paper - which of 58 CD-HIT clusters a Sir2 protein belongs to - is computed directly from the input sequence, i.e. leakage by construction. Neighbouring-gene domain calls come from GenomeNet Motif Search and the structures from AlphaFold, so those would be model outputs too. Only the 880 plaque-assay cells are a physical measurement, and they are in a figure.

existing_models.name: DefensePredictor (machine-learning classifier of prokaryotic anti-phage defense genes, Science 2026)
existing_models.score_and_split: Not verified by me; search results state it was applied to 69 E. coli strains with 42 experimentally validated novel systems, and to 1,000 prokaryotic genomes yielding ~3,000 clusters with no homology to known systems. No split or metric read from the paper itself.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Per the retrieved summaries, that a large uncharacterised defense repertoire remains - 15 protein domains in validated systems had never been shown to be defensive - so mechanism and specificity are unsolved.

backbone.name: ESM-2 (protein language model, small checkpoints run on CPU)
backbone.hardware: Laptop CPU would suffice for ~2,892 sequences

honest_claim_h3: No honest claim is available: with 8 defense systems measured against 110 phages and the results only in a heat map, any model would be describing four active systems, not learning a rule.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use defense-system and phage protein sequences to predict whether a bacterial Sir2-HerA system blocks a given phage
plain_idea.train_on: For each pairing, the sequences of the bacterium's two defense proteins (Sir2 and HerA) plus the phage's genome or its single-strand-DNA-binding protein. The paper supplies at most 8 systems x 110 phages = 880 pairings, and only 4 systems showed any activity.
plain_idea.predict: How strongly the system stops that phage, measured by plaque assay: phage is serially diluted tenfold on a bacterial lawn and the drop in plaque-forming units ('efficiency of plating') is scored. In this paper that number appears only as colour in a figure.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Labs that mine genomes for new anti-phage systems, and phage-therapy groups choosing phages that evade host defenses, would want to know which system blocks which phage without doing the plating. Even a failure would quantify how far sequence alone can go.

ml_idea: The only modellable idea here - predict phage restriction from defense-system and phage sequence - dies on sample size: 8 cloned systems (4 active) against 110 phages, with the measurements published as a heat map rather than a table. The paper's other large object, 2,892 Sir2-domain proteins sorted into 58 sequence-identity clusters, has a label computed from the sequence itself, so training on it would only relearn CD-HIT.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, not timed: ~2,892 short bacterial proteins through a small ESM-2 checkpoint on CPU is about an hour, and every table involved is under 10 MB. Compute was never the constraint.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the rows of measured antiphage protection that exist outside a figure. The methods say one representative locus per cluster (8 systems) was plated against 110 phages, so the answer is at most 880 cells over 8 systems - already below the floor before any file is opened.

verdict_reason: A mechanism paper, not a dataset: the only measured label (phage restriction for 8 systems x 110 phages) lives in a heat map figure, no data is deposited anywhere, and the one large label in the paper is a clustering of the input sequences.
